clinicalPearls: Skin thickening is confined distal to the elbows and knees (with facial involvement) and often follows years of longstanding Raynaud phenomenon
The CREST constellation summarises Calcinosis, Raynaud, oEsophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, and Telangiectasia
Anticentromere antibodies are the characteristic serological marker and correlate with the limited subset
Pulmonary arterial hypertension is the leading disease-specific cause of late mortality and may develop insidiously after many years
Regular echocardiographic and pulmonary function screening is used to detect pulmonary vascular disease before it becomes symptomatic
Digital pitting scars, ischaemic ulcers, and telangiectasia over the face and hands are common examination findings
Cutaneous change progresses slowly, so internal organ surveillance rather than skin score often drives management
reference.pathophysiology: Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis is a chronic autoimmune connective tissue disorder in which immune activation, small-vessel endothelial injury, and progressive fibrosis interact. Persistent vascular damage drives Raynaud phenomenon and a proliferative vasculopathy, while activated fibroblasts and myofibroblasts deposit excessive collagen in a distal-limited distribution. Autoantibodies, classically anticentromere, reflect the underlying immune dysregulation. Over years the vasculopathy may extend to the pulmonary arteries, producing pulmonary arterial hypertension, and to the gastrointestinal tract, causing oesophageal and gut dysmotility.
additionalInvestigations: Antinuclear antibody with anticentromere and extractable nuclear antigen profiling
Nailfold capillaroscopy to demonstrate scleroderma-pattern microvascular change
Transthoracic echocardiography to screen for pulmonary arterial hypertension
Pulmonary function tests with diffusing capacity to detect vascular or interstitial disease
Right heart catheterisation when non-invasive screening suggests pulmonary hypertension
Oesophageal studies for reflux and dysmotility when symptomatic
redFlags: Progressive breathlessness or reduced diffusing capacity suggesting pulmonary arterial hypertension
Critical digital ischaemia or non-healing ulceration risking tissue loss
Recurrent aspiration or severe reflux from oesophageal dysmotility
Rapidly progressive skin involvement suggesting evolution toward diffuse disease
reference.prognosis: Limited cutaneous disease generally follows an indolent course with better survival than diffuse disease, but the development of pulmonary arterial hypertension markedly worsens outcome. Early detection through surveillance and targeted pulmonary vasodilator therapy improves prognosis.
pitfalls: Attributing longstanding Raynaud to a primary cause and missing evolving systemic sclerosis
Failing to screen periodically for pulmonary arterial hypertension because skin disease appears stable
Overlooking silent oesophageal dysmotility and its aspiration risk
Assuming the limited subset never causes serious internal organ disease
references: EULAR recommendations for the treatment of systemic sclerosis
management: Vasodilator therapy for Raynaud phenomenon and digital ulcers, using calcium channel blockers, phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors, and endothelin receptor antagonists or prostacyclin analogues
Targeted pulmonary vasodilator therapy for pulmonary arterial hypertension, the leading disease-specific cause of late death
Proton pump inhibitors and prokinetics for oesophageal dysmotility and reflux
Regular echocardiographic and pulmonary function surveillance to detect pulmonary arterial hypertension before it becomes symptomatic
Management of calcinosis, telangiectasia and digital ischaemia, with wound care for ischaemic ulcers
Prompt ACE-inhibitor therapy should renal crisis occur, though it is uncommon in the limited subset
Multidisciplinary follow-up across rheumatology, respiratory and cardiology
